title: Forces and Newton's laws
goals: Work out weight from mass, and the resultant of several forces in a line
Use Newton's second law, F = ma, with the resultant force
Work out friction from the coefficient of friction and the normal reaction
Resolve a weight into parts along and across a slope
Work out the tension in a lifting rope while the load speeds up or slows down
summary:
A **force** is a push or a pull, in **newtons** (N). **Weight** is the force of gravity on a mass: $W = mg$, with $g = 9.81$ m/s². A 50 kg motor weighs about 490 N. Mass (kg) stays the same anywhere; weight depends on gravity.

The **resultant** is the single force that has the same effect as all of them together: forces the same way add, opposite ways subtract.

**Newton's laws**:

1. With **no resultant force**, an object stays still or keeps moving at a steady velocity.
2. A resultant force makes it accelerate: $F = ma$ (F the **resultant**, in N; m in kg; a in m/s²).
3. When A pushes on B, B pushes back on A with an equal and opposite force. The pair act on **different** objects.

**Friction** opposes sliding. Up to a limit it matches whatever is trying to slide the object; the limit is $F_{max} = \mu R$, with $\mu$ (mu) the **coefficient of friction** and $R$ the **normal reaction** (the surface pushing back, at right angles to it: on level ground, equal to the weight). Once sliding, friction is $\mu R$.

**On a slope** at angle $\theta$, split the weight: $mg\sin\theta$ **down** the slope and $mg\cos\theta$ **into** it (so $R = mg\cos\theta$).

**Lifting**: the rope's tension $T$ and the weight act on the load: $T - mg = ma$ (up positive). Accelerating upwards needs more than the weight; slowing down upwards needs less.

formulas.name: Weight
formulas.says: The pull of gravity on a mass.

formulas.name: Newton's second law
formulas.says: The resultant force on something equals its mass times its acceleration.
formulas.example: A resultant of 60 N on 20 kg: 3 m/s².

formulas.name: Friction
formulas.says: Friction matches whatever tries to slide the object, up to a limit of μ times the normal reaction.
symbols: the normal reaction from the surface (N)
formulas.example: 40 kg on the level, μ = 0.3: $0.3 \times 392 = 118$ N to start it sliding.

formulas.name: Weight along a slope
formulas.says: The part of the weight that tries to slide something down a slope.
symbols: the slope's angle to the horizontal
formulas.example: 20 kg on 30°: $20 \times 9.81 \times 0.5 = 98$ N down the slope.

formulas.name: Tension in a lifting rope
formulas.says: The rope pulls up, gravity pulls down; the difference accelerates the load.
formulas.example: 500 kg accelerating up at 0.5 m/s²: $T = 500 \times (9.81 + 0.5) = 5155$ N.

bench.task: Measure a coefficient of friction with a spring balance (or a luggage scale) and a block on a bench.
check: Weigh the block (or find its mass and work out mg)
Pull it slowly with the balance kept level; note the reading just as it starts to slide
Repeat on another surface, and with oil on it: what changes?

cards.q: You push a heavy crate across the floor with 50 N and it does not move. How big is the friction force on it?
options: Zero, because it is not moving
cards.why: It is not accelerating, so the forces balance: friction matches your 50 N exactly. Friction only reaches its limit, μR, when the crate is about to slide.

cards.title: Forces, mass and weight
cards.body:
A **force** is a push or a pull, measured in **newtons** (N).

**Mass** (kg) is how much stuff something is made of; it is the same on Earth or the Moon. **Weight** is the force of gravity on that mass:

$$W = mg$$

with $g = 9.81$ m/s² on Earth. A 1 kg bag of sugar weighs 9.81 N; a 50 kg motor about 490 N.

In everyday speech 'weight' means mass ('it weighs 50 kg'); in mechanics, weight is a force.
cards.more:
Why 9.81? Drop anything and, ignoring air, it speeds up by 9.81 m/s every second. Newton's second law says force = mass × acceleration, so the force doing that is $m \times 9.81$.

Lifting gear is rated by mass (a 1 t shackle), but the forces in the rigging are newtons: a 1000 kg load hangs with about 9.81 kN, more while it is being accelerated upwards.

Rough rule: 1 kg is about 10 N; 100 kg is about 1 kN.

cards.q: What is the weight of a {m} kg gearbox? Take g = 9.81 m/s².
cards.why: Weight = mass × g.

cards.title: The resultant, and Newton's first law
cards.body:
Several forces on one object can be replaced by one, the **resultant**. Along a line: forces the same way **add**; opposite ways **subtract**.

**Newton's first law**: with **no** resultant force, an object stays **still**, or keeps moving at a **steady velocity**. It needs no force to keep moving; it needs a force to change how it moves.

A conveyor running at a steady speed has balanced forces: the drive's pull exactly matches friction and drag.
cards.more:
This is the law that surprises people: we feel things need pushing to keep going. They do, but only because friction and air resistance keep trying to slow them. Remove those (a puck on ice, a satellite in space) and it carries on.

Numbers: a crate pushed with 200 N against 150 N of friction has a resultant of 50 N forward: it accelerates. Push with 150 N against 150 N: no resultant, so it carries on at whatever speed it already has (or stays still).

cards.q: A loaded trolley rolls along at a steady 1.5 m/s. What can you say about the forces on it?
options: They balance: the resultant is zero
The forward force is bigger than the friction
There must be no forces on it at all
Friction is bigger than the forward force
cards.why: Steady velocity means no acceleration, so no resultant force: whatever pushes it forward exactly matches friction. Forces are acting; they cancel.

cards.title: Newton's second law: F = ma
cards.body:
A **resultant** force makes an object **accelerate**:

$$F = ma$$

$F$ is the **resultant** force (N), $m$ the mass (kg), $a$ the acceleration (m/s²).

The most common slip is using one force instead of the resultant: always add up the forces (with their directions) first, then divide by the mass.
cards.more:
Numbers: a 25 kg crate pushed with 120 N against 45 N of friction. Resultant: $120 - 45 = 75$ N. Acceleration: $75 \div 25 = 3$ m/s².

Using 120 N alone would give 4.8 m/s²: wrong, because part of the push only cancels friction.

This is the same law as $T = J\alpha$ for spinning things: force and torque, mass and inertia, acceleration and angular acceleration.

cards.q: A {m} kg crate is pushed with {p} N against {fr} N of friction. What is its acceleration?
cards.why: Newton's second law uses the **resultant**: the push less the friction, then ÷ the mass.

cards.title: Newton's third law: pairs
cards.body:
When A pushes or pulls on B, B pushes or pulls on A with a force **equal in size** and **opposite in direction**.

The two forces act on **different** objects, so they never cancel each other out.

A motor pushes the floor down with its weight; the floor pushes the motor up with the **normal reaction**. A drive belt pulls the motor pulley; the pulley pulls the belt back.
cards.more:
Push a wall and the wall pushes your hand back just as hard: that is why your hand feels it.

Why do they not cancel? Cancelling only works for forces on the same object. Your push acts on the wall; the wall's push acts on you.

In rigging: a hook pulls up on a shackle; the shackle pulls down on the hook with the same force. Each part must be rated for it.

The weight of a box and the floor's push on it are not a third-law pair: both act on the box. They happen to be equal when the box sits still on level ground (first law); in a lift that is accelerating, they are not.

cards.q: A tractor pulls a trailer forwards. By Newton's third law, the trailer pulls the tractor…
options: not at all, if the trailer moves
cards.why: Third-law pairs are always equal and opposite, even while accelerating. The whole rig accelerates because the ground pushes the tractor's tyres forward more than friction holds the trailer back.

cards.title: Friction
cards.body:
**Friction** acts along a surface, against sliding. Up to a limit, it is **exactly** as big as needed to stop sliding; the limit is

$$F_{max} = \mu R$$

$\mu$ (mu) is the **coefficient of friction** (no units: about 0.1 for oiled steel on steel, 0.5–0.8 for dry steel on steel, up to 1 for rubber on dry concrete). $R$ is the **normal reaction**: the surface pushing back at right angles to it. On level ground, $R = mg$.

Once sliding, friction stays at about $\mu R$.
cards.more:
Friction is lazy: it only does as much as it must. A 40 kg crate on the level with μ = 0.3 can take up to $0.3 \times 40 \times 9.81 = 118$ N of friction. Push with 50 N: friction is 50 N and nothing moves. Push with 118 N: about to slide. Push with 150 N: it slides, friction stays at 118 N, and the extra 32 N accelerates it.

Why does R matter? Pressing harder on the surface (a heavier crate, or someone leaning on it) makes the surfaces grip harder. That is how brakes and clamping bolts work: more clamping force, more friction.

cards.q: A {m} kg crate sits on level ground. The coefficient of friction is {mu}. What horizontal force will just start it sliding?
cards.why: On level ground the normal reaction equals the weight; the limit of friction is μ times it.
cards.hint: $R = mg$ on level ground, then $\mu R$.

cards.title: On a slope
cards.body:
On a slope at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, split the weight into two parts:

- **down** the slope: $mg\sin\theta$
- **into** the slope: $mg\cos\theta$

The surface pushes back against the second part, so $R = mg\cos\theta$ and the friction limit is $\mu mg\cos\theta$.

It slides if $mg\sin\theta$ is bigger than that limit.
cards.more:
On flat ground ($\theta = 0$): $\sin 0 = 0$, nothing pulls it sideways; $\cos 0 = 1$, all the weight presses down. On a vertical wall ($\theta = 90°$): all the weight pulls it along, none presses it in.

Numbers: a 20 kg box on a 30° ramp. Down the slope: $20 \times 9.81 \times 0.5 = 98$ N. Into it: $20 \times 9.81 \times 0.866 = 170$ N. With μ = 0.4 the friction limit is 68 N: less than 98 N, so it slides.

A conveyor on an incline must hold the load against $mg\sin\theta$ (by friction with the belt, or cleats), and its drive must supply that force too, all the way up.

cards.q: A {m} kg block rests on a slope at {th}° to the horizontal. What is the part of its weight down the slope? Take g = 9.81 m/s².
cards.why: Down the slope: $mg\sin\theta$; into it: $mg\cos\theta$.

cards.title: Lifting: tension while accelerating
cards.body:
A load hanging from a rope has two forces on it: the **tension** $T$ up, and its **weight** $mg$ down. Up positive:

$$T - mg = ma$$

- hanging still or moving at a steady speed: $T = mg$
- **speeding up upwards** (or slowing while going down): $T = m(g + a)$, **more** than the weight
- **slowing while going up** (or speeding up going down): $T = m(g - a)$, less

Rigging and hoists are rated with this in mind: a snatch or a sudden stop can multiply the load.
cards.more:
You feel it in a lift: heavier as it sets off upwards, lighter as it stops at the top.

Numbers: a 500 kg load. Hanging still: $500 \times 9.81 = 4905$ N. Accelerating up at 0.5 m/s²: $500 \times 10.31 = 5155$ N. Stopping a descent at 2 m/s²: $500 \times 11.81 = 5905$ N, 20% over the static load.

A slack rope that suddenly goes tight is the worst case: the load is brought from moving to still in a fraction of a second, and $a$ can be huge. That is why snatch loading is forbidden in lifting operations.

cards.q: A {m} kg load is lifted with an upward acceleration of {a} m/s². What is the tension in the rope?
cards.why: $T - mg = ma$, so $T = m(g + a)$: more than the weight while accelerating upwards.

cards.q: A 40 kg crate on a level floor (μ = 0.3) is pushed with 200 N. What is its acceleration?

steps.ask: The friction limit. Is the push enough to slide it?
steps.show: $\mu R = 0.3 \times 392.4 = 117.7$ N. 200 N is more, so it slides; friction is 117.7 N.

cards.why: Reaction, friction, resultant, then F = ma. Check first whether it slides at all: if the push were under 117.7 N, the answer would be zero.

cards.q: Why does step 2 check whether the push beats the friction limit before going on?
cards.model: Friction is only as big as it needs to be, up to its limit. If the push were smaller than μR, friction would simply match the push, the resultant would be zero, and the crate would stay still. Taking μR off a push smaller than it would give a negative resultant, as if friction could pull the crate backwards, which it cannot.
points: Friction only matches what tries to slide it
Below the limit, no movement at all
Never let friction push it backwards

cards.q: A 20 kg box sits on a 25° ramp, μ = 0.3. Does it slide, and if so, how fast does it accelerate?

steps.ask: Does it slide? The resultant and acceleration.

cards.why: Split the weight, find the friction limit from the reaction, compare, then F = ma.

cards.q: A {m} kg pallet on level ground (μ = {mu}) is pushed with {p} N. What is its acceleration? (It does slide.)
cards.why: Friction at its limit μmg, then resultant ÷ mass.
cards.hint: Friction = μ × mg; resultant = push − friction.

cards.q: Friction on a 60 kg crate, μ = 0.4, on level ground. One line is wrong. Which?
lines: So 24 N will start it sliding
cards.fix: Normal reaction R = mg = 60 × 9.81 = 588.6 N, so the limit is 0.4 × 588.6 = 235 N
cards.why: R is a force, the weight, not the mass. Using kg as if it were N makes friction ten times too small. Units check: μ has no units, so μR must be in newtons, so R must be too.

cards.q: A {m} kg load is being lowered and is brought to a stop with a deceleration of {a} m/s². What is the rope tension meanwhile?
cards.work: Moving down and slowing: the acceleration is upwards: $T = {m} \times (9.81 + {a}) = {answer}$ N
cards.why: Slowing a downward movement means accelerating upwards, so the tension is more than the weight: the same as speeding up going up.
cards.hint: Which way is the acceleration when a falling load slows down?

cards.q: A motor sits on a bench. Which is the Newton's third law partner of the Earth's pull on the motor (its weight)?
options: The motor's pull on the Earth
The bench's push up on the motor
The motor's push down on the bench
cards.why: Third-law pairs are the same kind of force between the same two objects: the Earth pulls the motor, the motor pulls the Earth. The bench's push is a different force (a contact force) that happens to balance the weight here.

cards.q: A {m} kg drum sits on a {th}° slope, μ = {mu}. What is the largest friction force the surface can give to hold it?
cards.why: On a slope the normal reaction is only the part of the weight into the slope, $mg\cos\theta$, so the friction limit is μ times that.
cards.hint: R on a slope uses cos.

cards.q: A resultant force of {fres} N acts on a {m} kg trolley starting from rest. How far does it go in {t} s?
cards.why: Forces give the acceleration (F = ma); kinematics turns it into a distance.
cards.hint: F = ma for a, then suvat.

cards.q: A 2 t load hangs still from a crane. What is the tension in the hoist rope?
cards.why: Still, so T = mg = 2000 × 9.81 = 19 620 N. Tonnes are mass; tension is a force in newtons.

cards.q: An incline conveyor lifts {m} kg of load up a {th}° slope at a steady {v} m/s. Ignoring friction, what force must the belt give along the slope?
cards.why: Steady speed means balanced forces (first law): the belt must match the weight's part down the slope. The speed does not change the force (it changes the power: force × speed).
cards.hint: Steady speed: what must the forces do?

cards.q: A box sits still on the floor while you push it sideways with 30 N. The friction on it is…
options: μ times its weight, whatever you push
cards.why: Still means balanced: friction matches the push, up to its limit.

cards.q: A resultant of {fres} N on {m} kg. Acceleration?
cards.why: F = ma.

cards.q: The weight of a {m} kg motor?
cards.why: W = mg.
